title: Peter and Paul in Rome
hook: after Nero's fire, tradition says Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's journeys, and your line was he made tents. What ordinary work did you do as part of something bigger? Today the road ends in Rome. Day seven hundred fifty.

The book of Acts stops in a strange place. Paul has reached Rome as a prisoner, after a storm and a shipwreck, and the last lines in the King James Bible say: "And Paul dwelt two whole years in his own hired house, and received all that came in unto him." He is teaching, the very last words say, "no man forbidding him." And then the book simply ends. No verdict. No execution. Peter dropped out of the story long before. For what happened next to both men, the churches turned to tradition, and in that tradition the story runs through a fire.

The Roman historian Tacitus writes that after a great fire burned through Rome, the emperor Nero blamed the Christians, and had them put to death in cruel ways. Tradition places Peter and Paul in Rome in those years, and it remembers their deaths. Peter, it says, was crucified, and asked to be crucified upside down, feeling unworthy to die the way his Lord had. Paul, a Roman citizen, was beheaded with the sword. The New Testament doesn't tell either death. But it leaves two signs. In John's Gospel, the risen Jesus tells Peter, the one who had denied him by the fire: "when thou shalt be old, thou shalt stretch forth thy hands, and another shall gird thee, and carry thee whither thou wouldest not." And John adds: "This spake he, signifying by what death he should glorify God." Then Jesus says two words: "Follow me." The man who once said "I know not the man" is told he'll follow all the way. The second sign is a letter in Paul's name, written from prison to Timothy: "I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Not I have won. Not I was right. I have kept the faith. Two very different men. The fisherman who sank in the water and the tentmaker who once made havoc of the church. They argued once, in Antioch, face to face. And Christian tradition remembers them together, buried in the same city, honored on the same feast. Catholic tradition places Peter's grave beneath the church that bears his name in Rome. Whatever you make of the traditions, both stories come to the same place: faithful to the end.

Here's the practice: honor someone who paid for their conscience. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person, from any time or any faith or none, who refused to say what they didn't believe, and lost something for it: a job, their freedom, their life. It can be someone famous, or someone in your own family. Hold their face, or their name. Think about what it cost, and what they kept. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them. If you don't, simply honor them in silence. The bell holds the time.
Nero. The emperor under whom tradition remembers both Peter and Paul dying in Rome, honored together by the churches.
Your line: faithful to the end. Today, finish one thing you promised, even a small one, all the way to the end. Day seven hundred fifty.

howItsDone: Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches keep a shared feast of Saints Peter and Paul, and pilgrims visit the churches in Rome built over the places tradition names as their graves.

fork.setup: you're Peter, old now, in Rome. tradition says you're sentenced to be crucified like your Lord. what do you ask?
fork.reveal: tradition says he asked to be crucified upside down, unworthy to die the way Jesus did. the New Testament itself doesn't tell the story.

what a scholar hears: John 21:18–19 and 2 Timothy 4:6–7 point toward their deaths without telling them; the details come from later Christian writers.

notes: Editor pass: 'denied him three times' changed to 'denied him by the fire' (no count needed); misquoted 'I never knew him' replaced with Matthew 26:72 KJV; 'scholar' changed to 'tentmaker who once made havoc of the church' (Acts 8:3); Peter's grave now attributed to Catholic tradition.
Tacitus, Annals 15.44, is paraphrased: Nero blamed the Christians for the fire and put them to death cruelly. Confirm.
Upside-down crucifixion of Peter and Paul's beheading are attributed to tradition throughout (Acts of Peter; Origen as cited by Eusebius 3.1; Eusebius 2.25). Confirm wording.
'Peter, the one who had denied him three times': the count is in the Gospels (e.g. John 18; Matthew 26:34, 75). 'They argued once, in Antioch, face to face' paraphrases Galatians 2:11.
2 Timothy: 'a letter in Paul's name' is used because its authorship is debated among scholars; confirm the phrasing is acceptable to all churches.

'Honored on the same feast': the joint feast of Saints Peter and Paul (Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican calendars); no date given. 'Catholics see Peter's grave beneath the great church that bears his name in Rome' refers to St Peter's Basilica; confirm.
Original: τὴν πίστιν τετήρηκα (2 Timothy 4:7). Confirm transliteration.
Second editor pass: 'I know not the man' is Matthew 26:74 in the KJV (26:72 reads 'I do not know the man'); source ref corrected.

Audit pass: 'the line from both of them' implied 'faithful to the end' is a quotation; reworded. The 'unworthy to die the way his Lord had' motive is Jerome's (De viris illustribus 1); the Acts of Peter gives a different, symbolic reason. Both stay under 'tradition'; a Keeper may wish to check.
